\section[el orgullo]{el orgullo — pride}

\label{lesson:ES-C705-orgullo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to be moved, then the Spanish for to cry.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el orgullo}
\textbf{el orgullo} — \textquotedblleft{}pride\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mis hijos son mi orgullo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My children are my pride.}
\end{quote}

It can be good (pride in your work) or bad (too proud to say sorry).

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{orgullo} was borrowed from Catalan \emph{orgull}, which comes from Frankish \emph{urgōli} \textquotedblleft{}pride\textquotedblright{}, a Germanic word (EtymDB). French \emph{orgueil} is the same word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el orgullo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el orgullo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el orgullo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to be moved, then the Spanish for to cry, then say \emph{el orgullo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el orgullo mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Pride\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[orgulloso]{orgulloso — proud}

\label{lesson:ES-C705-orgulloso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to cry, then the Spanish for pride.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: orgulloso}
\textbf{orgulloso} — \textquotedblleft{}proud\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Estoy orgulloso de ti.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am proud of you.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Estar orgulloso de} — to be proud of. Feminine \emph{orgullosa}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{orgulloso} is built on \emph{orgullo} \textquotedblleft{}pride\textquotedblright{} with the ending \emph{-oso}, which makes adjectives; \emph{orgullo} was borrowed from Catalan \emph{orgull}, from Frankish \emph{urgōli} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la vergüenza]{la vergüenza — shame, embarrassment}

\label{lesson:ES-C705-verguenza}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for pride, then the Spanish for proud.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la vergüenza}
\textbf{la vergüenza} — \textquotedblleft{}shame, embarrassment\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
¡Qué vergüenza! Me caí en la calle.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{How embarrassing! I fell over in the street.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Me da vergüenza} — I am embarrassed (to). The two dots on \emph{ü} make the \emph{u} sound.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vergüenza} is inherited from Latin \emph{verēcundia} \textquotedblleft{}modesty, shame\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{verērī} \textquotedblleft{}to respect, to fear\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la vergüenza}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la vergüenza}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for pride, then the Spanish for proud, then say \emph{la vergüenza} again
\end{itemize}

\section[avergonzado]{avergonzado — ashamed, embarrassed}

\label{lesson:ES-C705-avergonzado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for proud, then the Spanish for shame.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: avergonzado}
\textbf{avergonzado} — \textquotedblleft{}ashamed, embarrassed\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Está avergonzado por su error.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He is ashamed of his mistake.}
\end{quote}

Used with \emph{estar}. In Latin America \emph{apenado} is also common for embarrassed.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{avergonzado} is built on the verb \emph{avergonzar}, made from \emph{vergüenza}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{verēcundia} \textquotedblleft{}shame\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[avergonzarse]{avergonzarse — to be ashamed}

\label{lesson:ES-C705-avergonzarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for shame, then the Spanish for ashamed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: avergonzarse}
\textbf{avergonzarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to be ashamed\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No te avergüences de llorar.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Do not be ashamed of crying.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Avergonzarse de algo}. Stressed forms take \emph{üe}: \emph{me avergüenzo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{avergonzarse} is built on \emph{vergüenza} \textquotedblleft{}shame\textquotedblright{} with the prefix \emph{a-}; \emph{vergüenza} is inherited from Latin \emph{verēcundia} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
